utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Good morning, everybody, and good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Prosecution -- from the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Ostojic. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. So we -- unless there are other matters that will be raised -- that are raised, today we have got two issues that we are going to hear submissions upon. You will recall -- I'll start with the first one. You will recall that on the 6th of July, we received a Prosecution motion for hearing and ruling regarding interviewing witnesses, that is, witnesses of the Defence, and this Monday -- last Monday, sorry, last Monday we directed that the issues raised in that motion be the subject of oral submissions this morning. More recently, that's on the 10th of July, Mr. Zivanovic, representing Mr. Popovic, filed a request for guidelines regarding interviewing Defence witnesses by the Prosecution. Basically, guidelines are requested which are on essentially the same issues as those raised by the Prosecution motion, and my proposal to you is that I open now the discussion on these issues, which will of course not only be limited to the Prosecution motion and the Popovic filing but any other related matter which you could have included in a separate filing and did not, but must be related to this subject matter, please. Who wishes to go first? I suppose since you initiated all this, Mr. McCloskey, you -- or Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I hate to disappoint you, but a full hearing I think may not be necessary after discussions with my friend this morning on this topic. The reason is after receiving my friend's filing last night, we read it, and the points he makes in section 2, background, paragraphs 3.1 and 2, were the key points in issue which is why we filed our motion initially. This position is new to us, that our right to interview witnesses is -- Defence witnesses, quote, is not in dispute and that there's no property in a witness. That was our main concern and point of dispute. While I'm not in full agreement necessarily with everything else in the motion, especially in the discussion session, I've talked to my friend this morning, and we think we may be able to have -- have further discussions and talk about our respective conduct with -- with the witnesses on both sides without necessarily needing any guidance or ruling from Your Honours. So I'm sorry about that, but once I sent case law to my friend last night, he sent me this motion last night and we've been talking this morning, so I think from our perspective the two main points are no longer in issue and the guidelines, which are new, we can discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is perfectly acceptable in relation to the Popovic Defence team, but I would like to know whether any of the -- first of all Mr. Zivanovic himself, but if any of the other Defence teams wish to make submissions on these guidelines because obviously this is not a case that relates only to interviewing Defence -- Popovic Defence witnesses but could apply to other Defence witnesses. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Nicholls just informed you about everything we agreed. Disputed issues from the point of view of our Defence were -- are in the paragraph 9 of our motion, and it is something that we'd like to discuss about, and we put all our questions in paragraph 11 of this motion. So I have nothing to add to this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Nicholls? Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I will be talking with Mr. Zivanovic later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any other -- of the other Defence teams wish to address it? Madam Fauveau first. She beat you, Mr. Bourgon. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since we are talking already about this issue, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that we are in special conditions of accessing Prosecutor evidence after their filing of 65 ter lists. We contact them, ask for authorisation, and after receiving their authorisation we contact their witnesses. We have so far never received such authorisation either because it was a sensitive witness or because he refused to talk to us. Otherwise, we are authorised to talk to the witness but in the presence of OTP. I am perhaps jumping ahead a little, but I want to know what happens after we file our 65 ter list. I would like to ask that the Prosecutor at this stage of the proceedings has the same conditions of access to our witnesses as we have to theirs. That is, for every contact with any of our witnesses they have to go through the Defence, which would inform them whether the witness is willing to talk to them and whether they would be allowed to contact them, or if the witness doesn't want to be interviewed by them, they will be able to have access to the witness after the witness finishes testifying here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who is going to respond to that? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what Ms. Fauveau has said is simply not true. We haven't put any conditions that they must contact -- go through us to contact witnesses on our list. That might be her understanding, but that's not been a condition that we've made, and it's not something that the other Defence teams have followed. The Nikolic team has interviewed a lot of our witnesses -- not our witnesses but witnesses on our list, and we find that out when we -- when they're here. We sometimes ask them have you been interviewed by any Defence or if we don't ask them, they say, yes, I've been interviewed twice, I've been interviewed before. We've had no problem with that. I think when the witnesses arrive here we sometimes get requests from the Defence and what we always do is, because the witness is here, we ask the witness if they want to meet, and many of the times the witnesses say yes. That's not up to us. We don't discourage or encourage or in any way try to influence a witness whether or not the witness should meet with the Defence, and we don't insist on being present. We ask the witness if they would like us to be present, and I think in perhaps all but one case, I might be wrong, the witness said no, that's not necessary, and then they've met very often -- at least in my memory with the Nikolic team and the Pandurevic team without us being present. And we -- once we get their witness list, I think the same conditions should apply. The whole point that I think we all agree on is that there is no property in a witness and that both sides are free to contact witnesses and try to talk to them. Now, there may be -- there may be instances of particularly sensitive witnesses or witnesses in one or another category where -- where there is a request from their side for us to notify them or -- and I don't think we have any problem with that, and we can talk about that if it's a special case, but in general, witnesses, as the case law which I was prepared to argue today before I got my friend's motion says that witnesses do not belong to anybody and either party is free to talk to them. And I'm not -- I didn't mean that when she said it's not correct that she was misrepresenting, but that's just not I understanding of the way it's been working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Ms. -- Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in these proceedings we received the first Prosecution witness list before the 65 ter list. That was in 2005, at the very beginning, and there were several hundred individuals on this list, and for each and every person on this first list we contacted the Prosecution to obtain authorisation from them, and from the very beginning this is -- or this was a mutual agreement between the Prosecution and ourselves. When the witnesses were in Bosnia, in fact, we did not have any problems, except in the cases of sensitive witnesses. But as far as I'm concerned, I never asked to have access to a witness who was a sensitive one. I never had any problems contacting witnesses, but we always did ask the office of the Prosecution for authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to be categoric about this, but knowing the jurisprudence of this Tribunal on -- even on this particular issue, I think you're talking at cross-purposes, because the jurisprudence has been quite clear that although there is no written rule that it should be so, the party wishing to interview a witness from the other side ought not to do it behind the back of the other party, and therefore that due notice should -- should be given. Together with the other principle that if the witness declines to give evidence, then you should not proceed, so -- not to give evidence, to give an interview, then you should not proceed. Do you wish to add anything to this, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think that's right. I think what I recall from early on is that we got e-mails before the trial started saying we intend -- from some of the parties saying we intend to interview the following witnesses, but it wasn't as though we gave permission at any point or said, yes, this one, not number 3. And so I think Your Honour is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Anybody else would like to make submissions? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, good morning Judges, good morning colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had prepared also some submissions this morning in relation to the Prosecution's motion and also addressing some of the issues raised in my colleague's response representing the accused Popovic, and I'd like to go through some of these issues that we'd like to raise with the Trial Chamber this morning, and I think we agree that what is mentioned in the Prosecution's motion in the first place, there is no property in a witness, I believe, Mr. President, that everybody agrees on this issue. And the second issue which I guess is also resolved already between the parties this morning and the question was, it is contrary to the rights of the accused for the Prosecution to meet with a potential Defence witness, and once again I think this is quite clear that it is not contrary to the right of the accused and the Prosecution has a right to meet potential Defence witnesses. However, our submission this morning relates to the conditions, and this was already introduced this morning, the conditions in which the Prosecution may and will meet with potential Defence witnesses. And firstly, we also agree with the -- what the Prosecution said in its motion, that the decision whether the witness will meet or not with the Prosecution or the opposing party rests with the witness. It's for the witness to say whether I consent or I do not consent to be interviewed by the opposing party. But even when we say that this decision rests with the witness, we must be sure and try to be as clear as possible that that decision is that of the witness and not that of the party calling the witness. And what we say is it would not be right for either the Defence to say Prosecution, you should not meet with the witness because the witness refuses. There has to be a mechanism by which the Court is aware that it is the witness who has decided that he does not want to meet with the opposing party. That's the reason why when a witness shows up in The Hague what the mechanism that we have adopted so far is we provide a letter to the Prosecution, and we ask the Prosecution, please hand this letter to the witness, and this letter basically explains who we are, what -- why we want to meet with the witness. We also mention specifically in that letter that it is a voluntary decision on the part of the witness, that he is not obligated to meet with us, and we also explain why we believe it is in the interest of the witness and everybody that we have this meeting before we proceed with the testimony. We also ask the Prosecution to basically give the letter, have it signed by the witness that he has read it and then the Prosecution will inform us of the decision of the witness whether to meet with us or not. And the advantages of proceeding in this way, the thing is, we know exactly that the answer comes from the witness on the one hand. We also ensure that there is no undue pressure by either party because we know the witness has seen why such a meeting would be appropriate and then he decides. The witness knows his rights, that he's not obligated to show up and he also knows specifically why we want to meet with him. Secondly, Mr. President, there are in our view in addition to the fact that it must be the witness' decision, that there are exceptions to the rule. It's not always the witness that may decide whether to meet or not. And the first exception to this would be, for example, if a party has -- sorry. The first exception is whether the Trial Chamber has issued a binding order at the request of the Prosecution, for example. And this is addressed in part in the Prosecution motion. If the decision issued by the Trial Chamber then the witness will have no choice but to meet with the other party. But the witness, even if the party has the obligation to show up if the Court issues a binding decision, the witness still has a right not to answer any questions, and that must be made clear to the witness. And I think that's the part that we are most interested here, because we want to avoid that any pressure, whether direct or implied or indirect, must be exerted on the witness to convince him to answer questions and to provide information. And this is where we have some concern. For example, if the Prosecution obtains an interview with the witness following a subpoena that was issued by the authorities of Republika Srpska, then the fact that a witness receives such a subpoena that he has to show up for an interview with the Prosecution on a certain date, we believe that this is a kind of indirect pressure where the witness feels that he must answer the questions of the Prosecution. And in that regard, Mr. President, I believe it is important to refer to the situation as it was described by my colleague Mr. Zivanovic in his motion. It is also our position that the people living in Republika Srpska, and especially in the Zvornik area today, are very scared. The situation described by Mr. Zivanovic is indeed accurate. The fact that there is a list out there that is being publicised in the media that there would be 28.000 persons who would be suspect and that everyone could be allegedly part of a joint criminal enterprise makes the people in the area very nervous and very scared, and in that respect, if they receive on top of this a subpoena to appear with the judicial authorities of Republika Srpska, then it might be very easy to influence them in the wrong direction. The second exception, Mr. President, to this rule that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me try to understand you better. What would these circumstances be? Because the only thing that can occur to my mind -- let's do it like this. Let me present it. Prosecution knows that there is Mr. XY who will be one of your witnesses. Okay. And they wish to interview him, and they will contact you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's not always the case but if they do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I'm presenting two cases because I want to see clear on what your submission is. They contact you. You contact your witness and give them all the information as to his rights, et cetera, and he confirms that he doesn't wish to meet with the Office of the Prosecutor. At that point in time, the Prosecution should back off, because if the witness is reluctant or refuses to meet with the Office of the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor as such does not then have the right to interview your -- your client. But it could well -- that would be interviewing your client, presumably, on the matters that relate to this case. Not your client, sorry, your witness. But it could well be that your witness, your witness, may in the eyes of the Prosecution be involved in other issues that they have investigated and that they may require him to be a witness for them in some other case. In that case, they will not be -- necessarily be interviewing your witness on the subject matter of this trial, but they would be -- or they would want to interview your witness on other -- other matters. At that point in time, they don't need to inform you specifically, although strictly speaking I would expect them to inform you that they are approaching that person. When you speak of subpoena, these are the two possibilities that I see. Where do you fit it in, because in the first case I don't see it coming in. I mean, how can the witness be subpoenaed to have an interview with the Prosecution if -- if he has refused within his rights to meet them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, I can even about a little bit further. I mean, in the area of a subpoena, the only -- only circumstance in which you could speak of a subpoena served on the witness to have an interview with the Prosecution, with the Office of the Prosecutor, is that there has been an ad hoc motion which we have never had. But in your submission you didn't actually state a subpoena by -- or from the Tribunal. You said a subpoena from local authorities, say the authorities in Republika Srpska. So I think you need to expand on this and explain to us what you have in mind. What would be the origin in such subpoena?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't -- I can't envisage, imagine, the Office of the Prosecutor asking, for example, Republika Srpska authorities to issue a subpoena to interview Witness X, who is a Defence witness, on these -- that matter of these proceedings, bypassing the Tribunal. I don't see it happening. I mean on the other hand, we've never had any such requests for such -- for the issuance of such subpoenas. So if you could expand a little bit on this as well, perhaps it would help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. This is exactly our point, that in the event there is a refusal by the witness, a potential Defence witness, to meet with the Prosecution, our submission is that the Prosecution should turn solely to the Trial Chamber to get a binding order if it believes it is necessary. Now, I'm advised that the word "subpoena" might not be the right word to use for what has been happening in the region. In order to meet with witnesses, the Prosecution has been using invitation issued by the police on paper and given to some -- to witnesses, but that's all witnesses, and the Prosecution will be able to confirm this. That's the way they have proceeded in the past. It's been difficult for them, as it has been difficult to us to meet with witnesses, and those papers are given to witnesses saying you are invited and you need to show up to the Prosecutor's -- to the Prosecution's regional office for an interview. Whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Presumably that invitation would not be issued or would not be made before the Prosecution has contacted you, and you have indicated that you will inform -- inform your witness, because otherwise, it would not be in conformity with -- with the procedure that our jurisprudence has laid down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's something different. It is happening, Mr. President, that the Prosecution will meet witnesses and will issue these invitations. In many instances we have witnesses who came here who testified and they referred to whatever the paper they received, whether it's a subpoena, whether it's a formal invitation, whether it's simply a strong suggestion that they show up to meet up with the Prosecution. And this has happened before with the Prosecution to meet its own witnesses. And what we're saying is that if in the situation -- what we want to avoid is that if in the situation the Prosecution exactly as you referred to talks to us, we speak to the witness, witness refuses, then the Prosecution should not use this kind of invitation to give that to the witness. It should turn to the Trial Chamber to get a formal binding order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. One question. This invitation that is issued by the local police, et cetera, are you stating that this is issued also when the Prosecution already knows that that person is going to be a Defence witness, because you could have two cases. You could have absolute ignorance on the part of the Prosecution whether that person is going to turn up as a Defence witness or knowledge already that that person will be a Defence witness. In the first case, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt, Your Honours, but one point is this is all somewhat hypothetical in the future because we don't have a Defence witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, and so it may be a problem that doesn't even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- arise but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do -- it doesn't arise as a matter of speaking but on the other hand, you have had several indications by the various Defence teams in relation to certain persons that they will be called as Defence witnesses, so at least as far as those persons are concerned you already have an indication even though you don't have the 65 ter list that we will have later on which Madam Fauveau referred to. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, would your position be different if the witness has not been contacted at all by the Prosecution but instead of contacting you, the Prosecution asks for the local police to ask the witness whether he or she will appear for an interview? So there's been no refusal on the part of the witness but the initial contact is made through the local police on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. Indeed this is our position. We would like to avoid the going to local authorities, that's the Prosecution going to the local authorities, does not take place before they speak to us if they know it's a potential Defence witness and after we've informed them that the potential witness refuses to meet them, then also that they do not refer to the local authorities, that they refer to the Trial Chamber if there is a problem. That's -- this basically is our submission, Mr. President. But there's a second exception to the rule, and unless you have other questions, I'll move on to my -- thank you, Mr. President. The second submission to the general rule that the Prosecution will meet with a witness if he or she accepts is that there's a possibility for a party to seek an order for protective measures concerning that witness. This was the case for Witness PW-101 and also PW-108. So these are exceptions to the rule. Now, should the Prosecution call the Defence and say we would like to meet with a specific potential Defence witness, they know that we've contacted the witness, they know that they've been informed that this is a potential Defence witness, in the event, Mr. President, that we inform the Prosecution that either it's our intent to ask for an order for protective measures or that we have already initiated the process by filing a motion to get an order for protective measures, in such a case our position is that the Prosecution should wait until the matter has been resolved by the Trial Chamber before proceeding with meeting that witnesses. And I don't think the Prosecution would object to such a procedure. Now, the reason I say this is that the four witnesses which are -- or the two witnesses, at least, which are referred to in the Prosecution motion and the Defence motion are witnesses who were referred to during a cross-examination recently, and for these witnesses the information that they provided is indeed very sensitive, and the witnesses are in a very delicate position, if I may use these words. For some of these witnesses, we indeed would like to apply for an order for protective measures to ensure that these witnesses will not be met by the Prosecution, but we have specific reasons for this, and we would like to apply. In this case, we had no time. We -- it was a rush for us to find these witnesses, to speak to them, to mention their names in cross-examination, and immediately on the same day both the Prosecution and Defence were looking for the same people. They found these people after having been given the names during the cross-examination, and that's when -- we never had any time to say, listen, please, we'd like to apply for an order for protective measures. Please wait until you meet them. There is no rush for the Prosecution to meet these witnesses exactly the day that we've met them or a few days thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What kind of protective measures do you have in mind when you refer to protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Protective measures that these witnesses would like to appear before the Trial Chamber with maybe a pseudonym --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I mean in relation to the Prosecution. You did not have in mind the delayed disclosure, because it is already disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is already disclosed and they know basically the gist of the information that these witnesses will bring. However, there are issues that we'd like to address the Trial Chamber as to why a specific witness should not meet with the Prosecution. Not meet. That's the measure. And why it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are arguing the -- you have poverty in that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No property. There is a reason why the witness should not meet with the Prosecution, because he might be involved, for example, in other matters that it would not be appropriate for him to meet with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me try and see clear in what you're submitting, because I'm not. Are you suggesting that once one of your would-be witnesses is granted protective measures such as pseudonym, facial distortion, and voice distortion, then there is no way the Prosecution can interview that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if he or she wants to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, if the person wants to be interviewed, there's nothing we can do about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- if the person tells --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- if the person refuses, then automatically there shouldn't be an interview. So what's the point of this submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because at some point when a witness refuses, the Prosecution may try by other mechanisms still to get to the witness. That's what we're trying to avoid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And your contention is that there are protective measures, such protective measures are operative also in relation to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because they are operative in relation to the general public.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The protective measures would be specific protective measures. For example, if one of these witnesses would like to be relocated and we have set in motion the procedure -- the procedure for the witness to be relocated and for the witness not to meet with anybody. Like, for example, we have not been authorised to meet with Witness PW-101 despite the fact that even after we tried to -- we obtained his name, we're not able to meet with PW-101 because the Prosecution did not want for protective -- protection reasons the Defence to meet with this witness. This might be the case, and we are dealing with some witnesses who can provide information that is quite sensitive, and there are reasons why these witnesses should not meet with the Prosecution. But I agree that this is a theoretical concept that today, that is it is speculation as of this day, but these are very sensitive issues and witnesses that we are dealing with. But all this to say, Mr. President, is that our position at this time, and we'd like to make sure that there's one issue we disagree in the Prosecution motion, and that is when the Prosecution says that because they've got the burden of proof they should be able to call witnesses during its case in chief. And what we are saying is that there is no link with the fact that the Prosecution has the burden of proof and that it should be in a position to call these witnesses that we've identified. The interests of justice requires that when there is information that is known and available it should be put to the Trial Chamber during the trial. It doesn't have to be put via the Prosecution. In our submission, this is why the Judges have the power to call witnesses at the end of the case that they're aware of and that have not been called by either party. Also the reason why the Prosecution may have -- there's the rebuttal phase which is provided for in the rules. So the interests of justice require that the information be put to the Trial Chamber as part of the trial, but it does not require necessarily that the Prosecution presents these witnesses during its case in chief. And what appears on the face of the Prosecution motion is that if we identified a potential Defence witness and they interview that witness, what is suggested in their motion is that they could call that witness in the Prosecution's case, and that's where we disagree. It doesn't have to be this way. There is no link between the two issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you -- have you never been in a case where the same person is witness for the Prosecution and also witness for the Defence? Because I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have, too, Mr. President. That's not -- again, maybe I'm not making myself clear. This is a witness that wasn't known to the Prosecution before. There was an agreement for that person to show up as a Defence witness in the case for the Defence. The person disagrees and does not want to meet with the Prosecution. In such a case there is no connection between this issue and the fact that the Prosecution would like to now call this witness during its case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you seem to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's two different matters to us, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also seem to have predicated, unless I'm misunderstanding you, that such a problem would arise because the Prosecution comes to the conclusion that that person is important for their case and they have the onus of proving the guilt in the first place. And you're saying that this notwithstanding, then they shouldn't have the right to bring that person as a Prosecution witness, or they shouldn't try to bring that person, because I'm not understanding you a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's not the fact that they do not have the right to bring that witness; it is that there's no connection with the fact that they may want to bring the witness and whether the witness will meet with them or not. But there's no connection between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And lastly, Mr. President, what we suggest in order to make it easy for all parties is that we proceed the same way for both the Prosecution and the Defence with the use of a letter that can be given to the witness. We suggest that this will ensure that we have a prima facie showing that there's been no pressure, that the witness understands that he does not have to consent to an interview, that the witness understands that has the right, even if he shows up for an interview, not to say anything. It is our experience in this case, Mr. President, that most of the people in Republika Srpska and Bosnia today are very little informed about their rights and due to this -- the rumours being spread around in the media, they are very sensitive to any invitation they get to provide evidence to the Prosecution. We feel that if we could proceed with such a letter, then this would solve all problems. The Court would be satisfied that witnesses and that there is a relationship of trust between the Prosecution and the Defence and that the decision whether to consent or not to consent to an interview is that of the witness and not of the party calling the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that's a lot and I'll try to respond it point by point and I hope I don't miss anything. But the starting point I would like to make clear is that to my knowledge, and I'm sure of this, the Nikolic team has never once contacted us before talking to one of our witnesses in the field, ever, and asked if that -- and asked them to contact the witness. And we haven't required that. He's contacted many of our witnesses many times and interviewed them without ever telling us or asking us or having anything to do with us, and we haven't had a problem with that. The second -- the first point he raised is the topics of these letters. Now, they have several times given these letters to us. I have always given the letter to the witness. I have told my friend that I'm not going to have the witness sign the letter that he's received it, because if I say I've given it to the witness, then he should trust me and that's good enough for him and I'm not going to force witnesses to sign documents to be returned to Defence, and he's accepted that. I don't think there's any need for us to give letters to the Defence because we don't trust the Defence otherwise to speak to the witnesses. I think we're all professionals here and I don't think there needs to be any suggestion that either side would -- would lie and say that the witness has refused to meet with you and that was not the case or has tried to influence the witnesses. So I will trust everybody on the other side with whatever they say if they represent to me whether or not a witness is willing to meet with us, and I would expect them to do the same. The -- the question about the subpoenas of witnesses, I don't think there are any exceptions to witnesses being available to either side, and there is no -- if a witness should refuse to meet with either side, the law on this case, which I think Your Honour was pointing to, the Halilovic appeals decision on subpoenas, that's from 21st of June 2004, is very clear, that a party may apply for a subpoena for somebody on the other -- another party's witness list, and the reason for that is as Your Honour said, the witness may be able to provide evidence for the party who wishes to speak to them, the party wishing to subpoena them, and that cannot be cut off by one party just placing them on the witness list. And if you look at paragraph 12 of that decision, it states to deprive the expecting party of such an ability to apply for a subpoena would hand unfair advantage to the opposing party which would be able to block its opponent's ability to interview crucial witnesses simply by placing them on the witness list. That can't be the law. It's not the law. It's true that that decision states that you can't subpoena a witness just to prepare for cross-examination, but if you believe and have a good-faith belief that that witness may be able to provide important information and that name is one that was not available to you before, you didn't have an opportunity to interview them before then, of course you can -- you can apply for a subpoena. Regarding the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would it not be different if the Prosecution case is already over?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, because it might be important for rebuttal. I think that it's true that if the Prosecution case is already over and it was -- it was solely to -- to -- to prepare for cross-examination, that might be right, but I don't think the law would change. It could very well be that the Prosecution needed to interview that witness even after its case was over, either for rebuttal or to bolster information that had already been provided or even possibly to ask theoretically to reopen on a certain limited point if the information was truly unavailable before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As far as the local authorities assisting, my friend has talked about how the witnesses are nervous, some of them, and again these are not in general witnesses who are on any list. We don't have a Defence witness list. But one of the practices we have is -- is to ask the local police to contact the witness and tell them that we would like to interview them, and there's two reasons for that. One, often we don't have any contact information and can't locate these witnesses despite looking in the phone book or something; and two, it is to make it easier on the witness, because then we don't - the investigator doesn't drive up to the front of their house in the village in a big UN vehicle which the witnesses may prefer just to be told that they should -- that an interview has been requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, are there any protocols in that region that require contact with the local authorities on the part -- if the Office of the Prosecutor wishes to interview someone? I know those are in place with some countries but perhaps not in that region?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, Your Honour, and sometimes witnesses when they have been asked by police to come don't come and say they -- the police say he can't come or this person can't come and then that's that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So it's not a mandatory requirement of the authorities in Republika Srpska, for example, that you contact them first before approaching a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't understand you completely. No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: It's something you do as a choice and for the reasons you've explained?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: That you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Namely because it's easier. It's easier that way for us to make contact. There's obviously a separate process, which is where we go through the RS liaison office and ask for a summons to bring somebody to our field office. That's not what we've been talking about and generally the interviews we've been -- that my friend has been discussing here are not conducted in a field office but just somewhere local, a local police station or somewhere. Moving to his argument on protective measures, I really frankly don't quite understand what my friend is saying. Protective measures have nothing to do with the other party's ability or right to interview witnesses. The one -- the one area where it would -- would affect that ability is -- Judge Kwon asked a question about delayed disclosure, delayed disclosure which is applied through the Court, then the other party is not aware of that witness until a certain time that -- so of course they can't contact them, but other than that there's no -- there's no basis for applying for protective measures as a way from shielding the witness from being interviewed by the other party. I mean, many of our witnesses have had protective measures and have been interviewed and either when they're here they've been asked if they would consent to an interview and they've said yes and then they've been interviewed. It's got -- it's apples and oranges. It's got nothing to do with it, and it sounds to me like just a way to try to shield the witness from access by the other party. The third point my friend got to was whether or not we can call witnesses in chief who arise through either cross-examining by the Defence or the Defence says we may call this person as a witness whether or not we can go interview that person and call that person in chief. And I think of course we can. That's recognised specifically in the Mrksic decision from 1st September 2006, paragraph 3, which I won't read that paragraph, but if you look at it, what it states is that -- that a party has to be able to and the Prosecution has to be able to during its case and even -- during its case it has to have access to witnesses that may be able to provide probative, relevant information that will help the Trial Chamber. There's -- there's nothing in the law and there is no rationale that I can think of that at some stage in the middle of the Prosecution's case when they learn of a witness who may be useful that they can't interview that witness and then call them. And we intend to do that. We've interviewed witnesses whose names have come up, names we've never had before. They have come up in cross-examination. We will go interview those witnesses and we will call these witnesses if we think -- we will apply to call these witness if is we think that they have important information. If we try to save that for rebuttal, I'm sure the Defence would argue, well, rebuttal can only be used for information that was not available that could not be foreseen and that doesn't -- it doesn't fall into that category because you knew about it in the middle of your case. And I think that can be argued further and fleshed out when we make a filing to add these people that we've recently heard about and talked to to our list. I think that's it. Again, in the end my friend talked about the letter. I don't plan on giving any letters to the Defence for them to hand -- when they give us our witness list we will cooperate with them, and I won't require my friends to give letters to the witnesses to sign and give back to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt, but basically I want to make some submissions on what Mr. Bourgon has said and I suspect he would like to the right to reply to what I'm about to say, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In essence I support everything he said in relation to the subpoena or the local police issue and what I submit in relation to that is that the Trial Chamber needs to be realistic and there isn't a level playing field in reality between how the Defence can act and react in relation to witnesses and how the Prosecution can act and react. The Prosecution have a well-established, well-oiled machine, for which we make no criticism at all, liaising with the local police and clearly that is going to impact on local people and local witnesses in an obvious way, and that is something that we would invite the Trial Chamber to take into account if it does lay down any guidelines as to how the Prosecution should behave come the Defence phase of the case in relation to the Defence witnesses, because frankly if I could use the military analogy, they have far more armory at their disposal in that regard. So far as Mr. Bourgon's second point is concerned, that -- frankly I have slightly more concern about. Could I endorse what the Prosecution said in their motion of the 6th of July at paragraph 6 where they stated that the Prosecution bears the burden of proof. It must be able to call witnesses during its case. And I'm not going to read out the rest of that sentence, but whilst as a matter of trite law, no doubt everyone in this room would agree with that, it is extremely important in practice, in our submission, and it's worth remembering at all times that the Prosecution bear the burden of proof and these defendants, all seven of them, don't have to prove anything at all, and they don't have to prove their innocence. And in that regard, what Mr. Bourgon is suggesting, and I know he don't mean this and I'm sure he doesn't mean this, might in some way suggest that the burden is shifting. It does not shift, it must not shift, and any suggestion in that regard must be rejected by the Trial Chamber. Could I just say this in fairness to my learned friend Mr. Bourgon and his client. Practically the issues that have arisen in this case that he's alluded to relate to his case, his team and don't relate, in fairness, to my client and the team in which I'm involved and therefore I can understand his concerns and that's something that the Trial Chamber may want to grapple with. Nonetheless, any suggestion that the burden shifts must be rejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Josse. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Before we hear from Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Nicholls, we had a question for you regarding the submissions that have been made. Once you receive the Defence list of witnesses, is it your position that you do not have to contact the Defence or notify the Defence regarding interviews that you wish to conduct of those Defence witnesses and that you can do so directly without notifying them? Or Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We clearly understood the President's -- I'm not sure it was a ruling but his feelings on that, and of course we will abide by that unless an issue meaning -- yes, if that's what he chooses, if that's what you choose. Whether we are legally required to do that, I would say that we're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Well, take it that we haven't ruled particularly on that, what is the Prosecution's submission as to whether or not you have to notify the Defence or make arrangements through the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We would say absolutely not. We have a duty under Dayton, a mandate to investigate these crimes, and these -- this will continue until the closing arguments of this case in order to respond to the defences and bring forward the case in as much truth as we can, and we will work with counsel and we'll of course abide by your rulings, but we do not feel that we are limited in any way by the Defence witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I could just add. I'm sorry I don't have the case law right at my fingertips, but I believe what is said in the law is that it's -- this would be a courtesy and it may be a good idea at times to avoid any -- any inference or appearance that pressure is being given but it is not required to go through the other party. And I think that's clear. And the Defence have not gone through us. They would do so if they thought that was a legal requirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this wasn't a joint case at the beginning. There were several ones. Miletic and Gvero was a separate case, and we had agreed with Mr. McCloskey to demand for authorisation. We did this on each and every occasion. The Statute of this Tribunal should be respected, and the Prosecution should conduct itself in the same manner as we have conducted ourselves. We have the right to prepare our case in the same way and under the same conditions as the Prosecution. We have the right to call witnesses for the Defence under the same conditions as the Prosecution. So I would like the Prosecution to inform us when they have our witness list. I'm not talking about the situation at the present but when we have our 65 ter list filed, I would like the Prosecution to realise that they have the obligation of contacting us when they want to contact our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, and then Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Maybe I -- you will allow me just to digress a little following up the question of Judge Prost on how the issues are regulated in the region with the local authorities. In its Official Gazette number 52, from 2001, 17th October, the Republika Srpska enacted a law on the cooperation with the ICTY, stipulating, or rather, regulating the issues that he would discussed today among others. Since I have this law in front of me now, it might help if I read Article 18 of that law governing the issue of legal assistance to the Tribunal, which says: "In addition to assistance in investigations conducted by investigators at the request of the ICTY, the competent authorities of Republika Srpska shall conduct certain investigative actions, collect information on criminal acts, perpetrators, and issue warrants," and I want to emphasise this, "deliver summons to persons in the Republika Srpska that were issued by the Tribunal." In keeping with the observation assisting practice and invoking this law, the local authorities, including the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, have so far delivered summons and subpoenas in this way. Under this law, there is no possibility to send official summons by the Defence through official channels into Republika Srpska, and that is where the difference between us lies. That is what I wanted to stress in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that if you wish to bring forward a witness that suddenly refuses to come other, you are precluded from asking the Trial Chamber to issue a subpoena? Because if that is what you are suggesting, I wouldn't agree with you. I don't know what you are suggesting, because I don't see any -- any inequality or lack of clarity of arms when comes to that, at least, between the two parties, the two sides. I mean, there have been requests in several cases for the issuance of subpoenas by the Defence, and they were -- they were granted. And they would have been executed by the authorities in Republika Srpska pursuant to what you have just read, because it says "collect and deliver summons to people in Republika Srpska that were issued by the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, you can conclude on this. Perhaps we could see better into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not for a moment did I say that Defence teams did not have opportunity to ask the Chamber's assistance to invite witnesses who otherwise refuse contact. Such situations have arisen, and I have encountered them in my work in the Tribunal so far and that is not in dispute. The provision that I have read, and it is set out quite clearly in the law, governs the issue of summoning witnesses by the Prosecution or by the Defence. Since this is the law on cooperation with the Tribunal, summons go normally through usual channels to the party. That is all I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, and then finally you will have your turn, Mr. Bourgon, unless you have changed your mind in the meantime. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try to deal briefly with Mr. Stojanovic. The Prosecutor does have the right to summons witnesses in her powers. I can't remember the Rule. And we have done that through the Republika Srpska. That's how we initially brought people to Banja Luka to speak to us. The Defence do not have that, that power, however -- and we also have a liaison officer that helps us find people and work with the local police, though I believe that liaison officer is open to the Defence and -- for both sides, both the federation and the Republika Srpska. And we will offer our assistance if they need to find someone or they need encouragement to the police to find one. However, would I gladly trade the RS police for their investigators, because as you know - and I won't go into the history, it's a little different than Mr. Josse said - the RS police are part of the perpetrators in this. And it's the light -- it's much different than it was two years ago, and so we are getting some cooperation, but it is not the situation of a well-oiled machine working hand in glove with the RS police. It's far from that; but again, that is not an issue. But I do offer our assistance where -- in any of these matters if we can give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Quickly, I just wish to reply to the points that were made by my colleague for the Prosecution. First, it's been said that the Defence has not contacted the Prosecution in order to conduct interview with Prosecution witnesses. I believe, Mr. President, that this is incorrect. With respect to witnesses in the field, we have provided the Prosecution, in September or October of 1995, with the list of all those that we wanted to interview. We have also received a response to this request, saying that go ahead, meet with whoever you want, inform us of the victims or the sensitive witnesses beforehand. And we have been confirming with this agreement. Secondly, when the witness shows up at the Tribunal, we have also requested, via the Prosecution before meeting with anybody, using the letter to which my colleague agrees is a good mechanism, and this way there has been less difficulties. Second point, I'd like to -- of course, I appreciate the intervention of my colleague, Mr. Josse, and I fully agree with him, and I thank him for raising the issue that there is no shift in the burden of proof. However, the argument that the -- I wish to make in this regard, the Prosecution, of course, has a right to call a witness as part of its case in chief. That is not the issue here. The issue is in the event a potential witness for the Defence has said, No, I do not wish to meet with the Prosecution; on the other hand, the Prosecution believes that it must call this witness as part of its case, those are two different things. And if the Prosecution wants to make a case that it must meet with the witness beforehand, despite his or her refusal, they have to turn to the Trial Chamber and not to local authorities. That's the second point, Mr. President. The third issue is concerning protective measures. My colleague says he doesn't see the point. Well, this is what happened in respect of Witness PW-101. Once disclosure took place, in conformity with the Trial Chamber's order, we were given the statements of this witness. From that point on, during that period of 30 days that we were given this material, we were not entitled to meet with the witness because the Prosecution had legitimate concern, because this witness was about to be relocated and for reasons to the witness they did not want anybody from the Defence to meet with the witness. What I'm saying is that the same could happen with a potential Defence witness; and in fact, Mr. President, we have one of the witnesses for whom we will be applying for both relocation as well as specific protective measures that that witness will not be contacted by the Prosecution. The name of that witness is not known at this stage to the Prosecution, and we will apply to also maintain as part of the protective measures to maintain the name, address, and location of this witness, until he appears before the Trial Chamber, for exactly the same reason as the Prosecution did with regards to Witness PW-101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, are we talking about PW-101 who appeared in February this year or Witness number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No, PW-101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who appeared if February.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed. The last issue is concerning the issue of the summons or the use of the local authorities. Again, our only submission is that if it has been indicated by the witness, by the potential Defence witness, that he does not want to meet with the Prosecution, then in such a case, if the Prosecution believes otherwise, they should turn to the Trial Chamber and not to local authorities. If they believe that there's a reason why they should be authorised to meet with the witness, then they should make their case and such -- where we will be able to respond to the Prosecution's argument, and the Trial Chamber will decide whether the Prosecution can meet or not with that witness, over the witness objection. And that's why I was calling about two exceptions to the rule; whereas, the witness decides entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, then you're not submitting that the Prosecution should be precluded from making their initial contact with the witness using the local authorities. Your concern is where the witness has already indicated they do not wish to meet with the Prosecutor and the use of local authorities at that stage, as opposed to an approach by the Trial Chamber. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is, as long as it's made on the -- on the assumption that the Prosecution has contacted the Defence and the Defence has informed the Prosecution that the witness does not want to meet with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So you're -- you're submission is twofold: First, that all contacts with the Defence witnesses should be notified to the Defence; and secondly, that if in the case of a refusal they can't resort to local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's exactly the point, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can -- yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to hark back to the very beginning of this particular debate, but my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic highlighted paragraph 11 of his filing of yesterday and said that that poses the various questions to which he requires answers. Now, I understand that Mr. Nicholls and Mr. Zivanovic had a discussion this morning but the rest of us were not party to that discussion. I would ask Mr. Nicholls in terms to answer those three questions in paragraph 11 so that we know exactly what the Prosecution's stance is in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, I am under the impression that he did refer specifically to paragraph 11 when he first spoke but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see we're four minutes from the break, I wonder if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just if we could the break now, I can -- I have to respond to Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Perhaps you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think 10 minutes once we get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can maybe talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a 30-minute break. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. A couple things first. The case I was trying to remember, which name I couldn't remember before when I talked about the notifying the other party would be a courtesy and may be a good idea but is not required is the Mrksic decision on Prosecution's motion to interview Defence witnesses of 1st September 2006, paragraph 4. That's what I was referring to. Second, Ms. Nikolic is correct and I apologise for that. They did send us back in 2005 a list of some of the witnesses on our provisional witness list that they intended to interview and our response was go ahead. Just to be clear, we did not set or make any condition that we would then contact each and every one of those witnesses and -- and get back to them. I think the response was a blanket response that they should go ahead. In terms of Mr. Bourgon's question about if they -- if they inform us that a witness refuses, whether we will -- whether we should be allowed to just use the local process, what I think we would intend to do is follow Mrksic, in general. We're courteous so much as we can be. However, what we will do is inform the Defence I believe of the witnesses that we intend to interview once we get their witness list and then we'll go out and try to interview them. And this is still far in the future, and I don't think any ruling needs to be made and we can still discuss this further. That has all come up just today, but I don't think we would be foreclosed by attempting to interview witnesses under those circumstances. I also want to be clear that I'm not being critical of the Defence teams for going and interviewing witnesses without telling us in advance or getting our -- our consent. What I meant was that we haven't heard from the field, we intend to interview your person on your witness list number X next Tuesday, and that's fine. We don't think that they need to tell us that they're going to go interview somebody who is on our witness list, and that's what I meant when I find out after the fact sometimes when the witness gets here that they've been interviewed once or twice by one or more Defence teams. Coming to my friend Mr. Josse's question regarding paragraph 11 of Mr. Zivanovic's motion which relates back to the information in paragraph 9, in general of course it's always okay to -- to inform a witness of any rights the witness may have, but it all depends on how it's done and at what stage it's done. And for instance, taking a statement from a witness, getting it signed, getting that information and then emphasising to the witness you don't need to talk to anybody else, you should have -- that could -- that could create in the witness the feeling that he ought not to speak to anybody else, but I don't want to go into that. I've spoken with Mr. Josse about that and he says that he's satisfied with my answer to him during the break. And the same as I discussed with Mr. Zivanovic earlier. I think it would be more helpful for -- for us to discuss with all the Defence teams what the guidelines, if any, ought to be rather than get into this at this point. And frankly without being cryptic and I don't want to get into it, we have had some concerns, but I don't want to get into that, and I think we should just discuss it amongst ourselves and we may be able to come to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, I think that should conclude -- no. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just a very quick point, just what my colleague just said. I would just like to know whether the Prosecution is willing to accept that if they do contact us about a witness and we inform them that the witness has refused to meet with them, will that be sufficient for them or will they go still and try to contact the witness. That's what we're trying to avoid, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would just say in this vacuum now I can't say that for all situations and all hypothetical situations in the future when we have a witness list that we would foreclose that. I'm not going to promise now or say now that we would never go attempt to interview a witness after that information. But that's again something that we can discuss and work on when we get a witness list and when we get to the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I think you already stated that you are all professionals here, and in any case, questions can be asked, can be put to the witness when he is here, and I don't think any lawyer would risk giving false information to the opposite party only to be exposed later on. So I would leave it for the time being. I wouldn't discuss that. I think that we can safely bring this discussion to an end here. Of course we will be coming back to you very shortly. The next item on our agenda for today is the issue -- next item on our agenda for today is the issue raised some time back and raised again more recently by the Prosecution and the Borovcanin team, as well as the Beara Defence team in relation to various issues related, concerning the tape recording of -- and transcript thereof of the interview which took place sometime back with Accused Borovcanin. We are going to deal first with the issue that was debated and which we -- as to whether the Prosecution should have the opportunity to play back excerpts of the tape recording, and then from then onwards we will move to other issues raised by both the Borovcanin team and the Beara team, as well by Mr. Josse and I understand also by Mr. Bourgon and -- yes, exactly. So before receiving submissions as requested, we wish to address the issue raised yesterday regarding the playback of the tape or parts thereof. The Prosecution, as we understand, proposes to tender through Witness Alistair Graham a tape recording and the transcript of a purported interview with Mr. Borovcanin. The Defence of Mr. Borovcanin have objected to the admissibility of the interview on several grounds and have given a very general outline of the basis for that objection during one of the hearings. The Trial Chamber is of the view that the procedure for consideration of the purported statement of Mr. Borovcanin should be in stages. The first step would be the examination of the issue of admissibility. We therefore wish to hear first and foremost of all direct evidence and cross-examination relevant to the issue of admissibility. Without prejudice to the issue of redactions to be dealt with in due course, for the purpose of this particular stage both the tape and the transcript will, for the time being, be marked for identification, however, with just one exception. We do not see any need for the playback of the tape in whole or in part at this stage with respect to the question of admissibility. The sole exception that I have just referred to would be where the Prosecution can establish that the playing of a portion of the tape is directly relevant to the question of admissibility and the point that would be demonstrated by such playback is not apparent from the transcript itself. If a portion were to be played back for this purpose, it would, of course, be open to the Defence on cross-examination to play other parts of the tape to demonstrate a larger or different context, and that is in response to the point raised by Mr. Lazarevic that playing parts could result to be out of context. Similarly, on redirect, if there will be one, the Prosecution may be permitted to play a part of the tape if relevant to the issue of admissibility and to a matter raised during cross-examination. So that disposes of the -- one of the issues raised by the parties as to whether during the testimony of Mr. Alistair Graham you should have the opportunity to play back parts of the tape recording at your choice. In other words, we are restricting that -- yes, we are restricting that within the parameters that we have established. Now, in order not to take you by surprise, which is not the style that this Trial Chamber adopts, yesterday after we had consultations in Chambers we instructed our Senior Legal Officer to contact you to give you prior notice on what we would like you to make submissions upon during today's hearing. I take it that this was -- or the e-mail was delivered to each and every one of you. If that's not the case, please stand up and inform us. So basically now I would like to approach the discussion along the lines of the points that were made known to you yesterday in Mr. Cubbon's e-mail. And the first issue that I would like you to discuss is an important matter, namely if the Borovcanin is -- Borovcanin interview is admissible, what probative value, if at all, does it have with reference to other accused in this trial, that is, other accused, other than Mr. Borovcanin. And I think this is the first issue that we would like you to -- that you should now address the Chamber. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I very briefly address the Trial Chamber, because I have one concern that I would like to share with the Trial Chamber, and if we can move into private session just to make sure that we are doing this properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session now. Before we proceed, because -- before we proceed, Judge Prost is reminding me, so that we lay the parameters of what the discussion should be limited to. Following the e-mail, Mr. Cubbon's e-mail to you, we are informed that Mr. McCloskey replied to Mr. Cubbon by means of another e-mail seeking guidance as to whether or not you -- we would want the parties to make reference to the Borovcanin interview specifically where Mr. Borovcanin mentions other accused or whether the parties should answer the questions generally without making a specific reference to the information in the interview. Correct me if I am wrong, but that's the information that we have. We haven't seen the e-mail. And then we are also informed that Mr. Josse interjected after Mr. McCloskey's e-mail, pointing out to Mr. Cubbon that the Defence, I take it his Defence team, would --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right. I should have made that clear in the e-mail and I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That the Defence for General Gvero would wish to make oral submissions on the question raised by Mr. McCloskey prior to the Trial Chamber making any decision on it. So our decision on this is that on this first point that I've raised with you the debate should be in general terms and not with specific reference to the bits and pieces or parts of the Borovcanin statement as they may or may not relate to other co-accused in this case. So it's a generic debate on a legal level that we are expecting to -- from you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I -- that's what I thought the answer was since you do not have this statement yet, and so that's what I have been prepared to deal with this generally, and my comments today will be -- will try to be brief, though you have touched on a rather significant issue that, as you know, is a matter of among all three of the large cases before us, Prlic, Milutinovic and our case. I'll speak briefly to that, but let me go down your list as you've said. If the Borovcanin interview is admissible what probative value, if any, does it have with reference to other accused other than Mr. Borovcanin. Now, I don't want to overlawyer that question, though I'm sure I have. I have basically two kinds of answers for this in case -- I'm not sure exactly which one you were looking for. But when I look at the term what probative value, I look at the meaning the term probative value, and that is evidence that tends to prove an issue. So is there anything in Mr. Borovcanin's that tends to prove an issue related to one of the co-accused. The answer to that is clearly yes, and again I won't get specific, but I think it's a good idea when looking at an interview like this to roughly divide it into three parts. There is -- there's information, background information, back -- personal background to the accused, background to his history, structural information about his -- his police force, things of that nature. I would say that's roughly category one. Category two would be information related to events around the indictment, the factual events, the fall of Srebrenica, where troops went, things like that that are more closely related to the events and the charges of the indictment. And then third, there is information that would go to the acts or conducts of other accused, evidence that would tend to prove issues. Presence at a particular location, things like that. So I think the answer to the question of does it have probative value, the answer is a resounding yes, it does, absolutely. Now, if the question is more general, can a statement such as this have value for you to be used against other accused, which I think is the big issue that I referred to, and we've talked about it briefly, the answer to that again is yes. And you have heard my view in the Jokic trial, and you've heard briefly what the Prosecution's view is now, and the current view is that yes, the interview of Mr. Borovcanin should be and can be used for all three categories that I have mentioned. Now, in my view the -- this is an issue that involves the fundamental fairness, and I think as it's laid out most simply in Rule 89(C) and (D), where, as you're aware, a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value on the one hand, and (D) the Chamber may exclude evidence of its probative value if substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. So the balance that the Trial Chamber needs to make is we have probative -- we have evidence of probative value, yes. In using that evidence does that take away from the other accuseds' right to a fair trial. And I think that now takes us into the legal argument, and it's a legal argument that I can share briefly with you, though I think it's an argument that I think all sides would like to brief thoroughly, because as you know, it will be -- it will involve issues of international law, issues of national law, issues of Tribunal law, and is -- obviously an extremely significant issue that will soon be in the Appellate Chamber in one of our -- in one of our cases very soon because I think it's the Prlic case that there's actually a motion on this very point. Now, under 89(C) and (D) the Trial Chamber has broad discretion, as you know, and that is those of us from the common law systems know that the right to cross-examination is partly what drives this issue, but the civil law also has similar fairness issues and many civil law countries also do not allow a co-accused statement though there are some that do, and this is a complicated issue and it will take all of us lots of digging to give you a good -- a good representative sample of this. One recent case I think is helpful for us, it's the Martic appeals case where you may remember an important witness for the Prosecution, Mr. Babic, was on the witness stand and was making comments that directly implicated the accused and then he died. And so the Court of Appeals had to decide on that issue, and they did decide that cross-examination was not an absolute and they did allow that evidence to go in uncross-examined. And one other area I'd ask you to look at is the court in -- the Strasbourg court and the European Court of Human Rights has dealt recently with this issue in September 2006 ruling called Carta versus Italy where they had a similar situation and chose to allow the co-accused's statement to be used. I won't get into the facts on that. I'm really probably not qualified to. I haven't had a chance to read it thoroughly, but I think it's something -- an interesting case, and is the kind of international case that we should be looking to because of the international nature of our Tribunal. And so without going into the details of this very interesting and complicated issue, I would leave it -- leave it at that, though I would say -- of course the most difficult choice in my view for the Court is looking at the area of acts or conduct: Is this something that should be not admissible or it should -- just a matter of weight. Clearly a statement of one accused, uncross-examined, that blames another accused or says something about an accused is a matter that the Court I'm sure would be looking at with -- with great -- a great critical eye and would be able to give it the appropriate weight, if any, it needed. And that's -- that's to be expected, and I think this is an area of law throughout the world, especially in jury trials, where jurors are -- are normally instructed to take this kind of evidence or evidence of a co-accused or a co-partner with some -- with a critical eye. Though the background evidence that I spoke of or the evidence related to crimes or the troop movements, these sorts of things, I think they're going to -- they will have more indicia of reliability and I don't see any reason why a Court can't consider those and give them the weight they find appropriate.
