So I would ask you to look at all three areas and consider all three and give the weight that you find appropriate. This issue will come up with the -- I believe it's 94 quater issues where we have had witnesses that have recently died. Miroslav Deronjic, for example. The same issue will come up, because he will testify -- or he has testified relating to the acts or conduct of the accused. He's also testified about the -- the famous July 17th document that you may recall Major Franklin having to testify to that is something that doesn't go directly to acts or conduct. So this issue is not going away. We will be filing a quater motion very soon. But those are some of the cases, and this will be the Prosecution's position, though the Prosecution's position is in the middle of being formatted Prosecution-wise -- wide. So I don't believe it should change much from what I have said, but as you know and as you can see from my position in an earlier case, it is a changing area of the law. So I can then -- if there is any other questions, I can go to question two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, more or less we anticipated all this yesterday when we were discussing, but we went a bit further than that, and I will be asking you a question that we discussed amongst -- or relating to an issue that we discussed amongst ourselves yesterday. Judge Prost also will raise another matter with you relating specifically to the kind of Tribunal procedure that we have here, and I understand also Judge Kwon would be putting his. My question to you is the following: In your mind in making this submission, do you -- or are you making any distinction at all between the fact when the person making the statement, in this case the accused at the time who was a suspect, but the accused making the statement ultimately decides to give evidence and, therefore, would be subject to cross-examination, and the other case when he decides not to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this submission I am assuming this -- Mr. Borovcanin would not testify, because I have no way of knowing at this point whether he would or would not. And aside from asking Defence counsel, but Defence counsel, that's a decision they have to make and it can change. So I have assumed for this argument that he is not testifying, though he may, and of course if he does testify he will be open for cross-examination by everyone and the door is all open and no one would have any objection, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon -- Judge Prost. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have any submissions as to whether the facts that the Tribunal, unlike some of the jurisdictions where such statements are not admissible against co-accused, in this Tribunal hearsay is admissible, albeit there is a weight consideration obviously. But is there -- do you have any submissions on that distinction and the distinct nature of this Tribunal in terms of hearsay with this statement in essence constituting a hearsay out-of-court statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And as a matter of fact, the foundation of my argument that you should especially look to the first two categories of material that don't go to the direct acts or conduct of the accused is not that different than 92 bis evidence and as an exception to the hearsay rule, and so I think that's fundamental, which I should have mentioned. The fact that hearsay is admissible is fundamental to the entire argument that I am making. I went to the most fundamental cross-examination and the fact that some civil law countries share that same concern under basically a different theory. But this -- this entire argument is based on -- in part on the fact that hearsay is admissible, especially all the information that does not go to the acts or conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not necessarily, but my question was just treated by Judge Prost's question. But when you say this is hearsay evidence, this is hearsay evidence to be heard by one of the investigators of the statement of the accused which you will tell about the story about the other accused. So you follow so far then. If it is to be allowed, then we should allow the Prosecution to call the investigators, not the crime base witnesses to hear any crime base or even the act and conduct of the accused. So it's not only the hearsay matter but the -- fundamentally the fairness issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that had this been an interview where Alistair Graham had interviewed him and then taken notes on -- on what was said and the -- the accused had -- and didn't sign the notes, what we call an information report, what is a traditional way of taking statements in many countries. Had that been the case, I think what you're saying would be more of a concern because you're really going so much on the integrity of the -- of the investigator, which is fine and good and they have credibility. And we -- sometimes we will be providing evidence that -- that a victim or a witness could have testified through the investigator. You'll see that down the road. And in many cases, especially with crime base issues, that's appropriate and investigators are credible, and I think you'll be satisfied with that evidence. And if that's all we had, I think your -- your decision would be more difficult. But I think the rules protect us from having to make that particular decision because they require that this be audiotaped. And so we're really -- while it's coming through Alistair Graham, mostly Alistair Graham is here to prove to you, to meet my burden that this was done according to the rules and it was done freely and voluntarily, and the words will be the words of the accused and -- and Mr. -- and the investigators making the interview. So I don't think it's a question that this would be a problem that would -- that would affect the rest of the system or the -- or the Tribunal as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question was whether what we will hear from Alistair Graham is related -- rather, related to the issue of admissibility than the content of Mr. Borovcanin's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that is my understanding, and having listened to your recent ruling, we would be -- and it will be Mr. Nicholls that will be asking Mr. Graham the questions. It would fundamentally be the background of the interview: Did you interview him? Did you do it according to the rules? Did you make him any offers, any promises? Did he agree to waive his rights? And any particular issue that the Defence may raise that we need to -- need to deal with. There may be an exhibit. Is this the summons that was served on him indicating he was a suspect? Why did you say possible suspect in your -- in your reading? That kind of thing. And I wouldn't expect any content at all or probably based on your ruling any need to play the -- any part of the -- of the transcript unless at some point someone suggested that he -- that Mr. Borovcanin was coerced or pressured in some way, and then we might want to play part of the interview that showed the opposite. But I really doubt it. I -- I've gone through hundreds of these sorts of things in other courts, and if it's anything like those, it should be brief and legal and it shouldn't involve much of the interview itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I think I'm going to do the round because -- yes. Who would like to go first? In relation only to this first posit, yeah. Now all of a sudden, three, four stand up. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I completely agree with the fact that the question of the probative value of the statement of Mr. Borovcanin's interview has first to be resolved. If this statement has no probative value, it can't be admissible. The rules are very clear as far as this issue is concerned. In accordance with 89(C), only evidence that has probative value and that is of relevance can be admitted. Also pursuant to 89(C), Rule 89(C), any evidence the probative value of which is inferior to the request for a fair trial must be excluded. So this interview and any other forms of evidence, if it has no probative value or if the probative value is outweighed by the need for a fair trial, well such evidence has to be excluded. I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that in the Blagojevic case, there was a similar issue -- or rather an identical issue. It relates to admitting Mr. Jokic's interview. In this case the Chamber ruled that any interview with a suspect has a relative value because it's quite natural that a suspect doesn't want attention to be focused on him and will try perhaps to exaggerate the guilt of others. In this particular case and in Mr. Borovcanin's interview the Prosecution yesterday told us that on occasion there were interpretation problems, as far as I have understood, certain problems were resolved, given that there was a revised translation that was subsequently done. But the problem of interpretation affects to a significant extent the veracity of Mr. Borovcanin's statement, because during this interview the interpretation was sometimes incorrect. The Prosecution told us quite clearly that on occasion the question put had been altered as a result of the interpretation. So we have a question and an answer that does not completely correspond to the question posed. In my opinion, this is extremely important, because Mr. Borovcanin's answer could concern a different event or a different date than the events and dates referred to in the question and sometimes one may have the impression that Mr. Borovcanin is being evasive or is failing to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I hate to interrupt you like this, Madam Fauveau, but the -- our concern is that we try to approach this first question to you in a -- from a general approach and not specifically with reference to particular parts of the Borovcanin team, et cetera. So you could -- we appreciate what you have, of course, submitted, but we suggest that you try and go straight to the general issue from a general point of view as to whether legally a statement by one accused against another co-accused should have any bearing, any probative value vis-a-vis that co-accused or co-accuseds.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'll follow your advice. All I wanted to say is that I believe this question of interpretation is a general issue, but I will move on to another subject. Obviously in my opinion an interview of a co-accused can't be admitted in this case against other co-accused who also don't have the right to cross-examine. I believe that the reference to Mr. Babic's case is quite different because Mr. Babic testified before the Chamber and in fact -- well, there was no cross-examination, but at least there were certain procedural guarantees. As far as this interview is concerned, well, it's a Prosecution interview, and there is no guarantee that this interview fully corresponds to a statement that would have been given before the Court. What I want to say is that I don't want to reproach the Prosecution for having conducted this interview as part of their investigation in order to be able to use the material in the course of their investigation, but if such an interview had been conducted before your Court, before your Chamber, you would never have allowed a question to be put five times or a question to be leading or for the Prosecution to provide advice, perhaps in good faith, but advice provided to Mr. Borovcanin. What I want to say is quite simply the following: The form of the interview is such that in my opinion it should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. She's going beyond the question what you've already asked her and she's attacking the interview, which is -- I'm not sure she has standing to do that either and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, Madam Fauveau, please, we made it clear that we want submission -- submissions on this issue, namely just one simple straightforward legal question. In this Tribunal, if a -- an accused person makes a statement which -- in which he attributes acts or conduct to other co-accused, does his statement have probative value? Can it be used, basically, if it has probative value at the end of the day, against the other co-accused? This is what we want to hear, and the reason is that as has been stated, the practice varies from country to country. The issue as such is relatively new to this Tribunal, and we would like know what your respective positions are so that we will then be able to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I completely agree with you, but the problem is that the form of a statement, of an interview, is also an important matter when it comes to deciding on the probative value and when it comes to deciding on its admissibility, a priori, I am against this because I don't have the right to cross-examine this witness. I don't have the right to examine, to cross-examine this form of evidence. If I can just say that I'm against this without explaining why, I'll stop there, but if we're referring, for example, to civil law countries, well one must be aware of the fact that such a statement doesn't even -- such a form -- such a statement in such a form don't exist in civil countries. We can't refer to continental countries, because there, everything is before Judges where there aren't any leading questions, there aren't repetitive questions. An accused doesn't follow the framework of questions and responses. He just gives a statement, narrates a story and finally if there are questions at the end, it's within the framework of a certain procedure. There are no leading questions, there are no questions that raise the issue of the form of an interview. So that's why I wanted to tell you that my thought that this interview, apart from my general objection that -- apart from my general objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, the interpreter seems to have a problem -- grasp with you, but I understand your point, but I think we may come to the issues you like to discuss at the second point, but for the first point, we'd like to confine the discussion to the issue whether the -- one of the state -- statement of one of the accused can be used at all against the other co-accused as a general matter of law when the accused is not to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I agree a hundred per cent with Judge Kwon, and the question as to the form resorted to by the Office of the Prosecutor in taking down statements is beyond discussion now. I mean, that has never been in dispute here. It's not required. So I don't think you should concentrate on that, although it may have its consequences, of course. But you should concentrate basically on assuming that the statement has been taken, assuming that the statement has been taken voluntarily and according to the rules, assuming that in that statement there are excerpts or there are parts where other co-accused are attributed responsibility or there are -- there is information in relation to other co-accused, can those parts of the statement of the accused be used by the Trial Chamber in regard or vis-a-vis other co-accused. This is what we need you to address for the time being. And the reason is very simple. It's not yet been finally determined by -- by this Tribunal. The only decision that there is bypasses really the issue and doesn't address it, and -- and we are a Tribunal that is international and does not necessarily stick to one or more of the systems existing in the world. So this is why we seek your contribution in this debate so that we will come out of it more enlightened than we started in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. In my opinion it can't be used. Quite simply, and I'll be very brief, because we don't have the right to cross-examine, and there are no procedural guarantees. And I'm not referring to Mr. Borovcanin's interview. I'm referring to this case in general. The Prosecution conducts an interview with an accused. There are no guarantees, no procedural guarantees that are necessary in all systems and that includes this system. There are no procedural guarantees when the Prosecution conducts an interview and when it comes to the rights -- the protection of rights of others. In the Prosecution's interview we are dealing with the rights of the person interviewed if the person is a suspect, but there are no guarantees so that the rights of others are respected and so that this statement, this interview, fully corresponds to the truth and fully corresponds to the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I put to you the same question I put to Mr. McCloskey. What if ultimately you -- it will be possible for you to cross-examine the -- the accused making the statement? Would your position change? Because if the basis of your position is merely the fact that there is no right or no possibility for you to cross-examine the accused making the statement, then if that possibility emerges or comes into being, would the legal scenario change or remain the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, yes. Yeah, the solution would be different, but not completely different, because in this case the accused would become a witness, and I believe that this preliminary interview could be used as any other preliminary statement of any other witness. Insofar as the party calling the witness, it would be in a limited scope and for us it would be in a totally different scope. If Mr. Borovcanin chose to testify, he would be called by his counsel, and obviously the Prosecutor cross-examining this witness could use this interview, which would be logical. But as long as we don't have the right to cross-examine, I believe there is no legal ground that would allow the use of this interview with respect to the other co-accused without prejudice to their rights. I just want to add that I'm not only concerned about the acts and conduct of the co-accused but the total picture that this creates, because it deals with the factual basis of certain criminal acts that our clients are charged with. And if we don't have the right to cross-examine and this picture created by the interview is false, is not true, I believe it would create -- it could create irreparable damage to the other co-accused even if it doesn't directly concern their acts and conducts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I was listening in French. I'm sorry. My apologies. Can you tell me what difference you would draw between this out-of-court statement, hearsay statement, where the maker of the statement is not available for cross-examination, assuming that's the case, and other out-of-court hearsay statements where they are admissible, albeit you don't have the opportunity to cross-examine the actual maker of the statement since hearsay is admissible in this Tribunal? What distinguishes this particular statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prost, I believe this Tribunal of course admits hearsay evidence, and I'm completely used to that, although not in my country, but the difference -- the distinction I wanted to draw -- I'm sorry, I can't see you -- goes to the details of this particular interview. That's why I'm going into the details, because I believe them to be very important. And they distinguish this particular interview from other out-of-court statements that the Court may admit without allowing cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Who wishes to go next? Mr. Josse? I mean, I'll let you fight it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Josse. I will be very brief. Under question one whether the interview is admissible what probative value it has against any other accused that are mentioned or might be mentioned, none. Absolutely none. Very simple. Because this is an unsworn statement made by a co-accused at a time that he was either told he was a suspect or was going to be indicted or he believed that he was going to be indicted. Further, this statement was made long after the joint criminal enterprise had ended. It wasn't made in the course of any joint criminal enterprise if one even existed. Next, it's obvious that an individual who is giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor or to the government or to the Prosecutor here or in any other country knowing that he may get indicted has a very large motive to shift the blame from himself to others to protect himself. That -- the credibility of that declarant, the statement he makes will absolutely be untested. If it's admissible and if it is admissible and given probative value against any accused who might be mentioned in that statement, again no chance to cross-examine, no chance to confront the witnesses against them, no chance to test the credibility of the declarant. Since we can't, Your Honours, we can't cross-examine this paper, that means that my client or any other accused here in this courtroom who is affected by the statement of Borovcanin, if it comes in, it means that their right to effective assistance of counsel has been denied. And further and lastly, Your Honours, and very importantly, if you make this ruling, we won't have the right to confront. We won't have the right to cross-examine. We won't have the right to the credibility and test. And what that will do, it will have -- effectively it will shift the burden of proof from the Prosecution to the accused. That's my submission as short as I can make it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also have failed to address the two points or the three points that were raised by us. Number one is precisely the eventuality of your being able to cross-examine the accused, would that change the scenario? Number two is this Tribunal hearsay is allowed. A statement made or released by one accused in the parts that he mentions other accused, other co-accused, those parts are hearsay, and that would be hearsay and therefore would, as explained by Judge Prost, be admissible under our rules of evidence and procedure. And thirdly, the point also made by Judge Kwon. So you can address these issues. Would the scenario -- for example, is it important at all for you or to you the fact that while in your country, for example, hearsay, and in my country hearsay evidence would not be admissible, in this Tribunal it is. Does it have any importance for you or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, no. It doesn't, Your Honour, and I'll tell you why. I thought I did. Let me explain it one more time. This is a special kind of hearsay. This is a hearsay coming from a co-accused. This is hearsay that is obviously coming from a person who has a motive, a very distinct motive to shift the blame from himself to others. So for that reason it's different. Now, the other question. If the declarant, Mr. Borovcanin, decides to take the stand then we wouldn't be having this discussion in my opinion because he would be subject to cross-examination, confrontation, and we could test his credibility. However, however, I think you must assume that he will not testify, and therefore you must assume if you allow this, you do what the Prosecution asks of you, then my client and many other accused, perhaps, are going to lose their right to a fair trial, their right to confront and cross-examine, their right to effective assistance of counsel and the burden of proof will be shifted from the Prosecution to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the purpose of the whole -- of the question that was put to you basically is this: Do you allow -- a question put to you, all of you, was if the Borovcanin interview is admissible -- everything is predicated on this, okay? What probative value, if at all, does it have with reference to other accused other than Mr. Borovcanin? The question is: If the fact as to whether Mr. Borovcanin will testify or not is unknown and will remain unknown until we come to the crucial moment, if that is the case do you allow for the possibility from a legal point of view that any decision as to whether the statement made by Mr. Borovcanin in relation to vis-a-vis other co-accused can remain in limbo until the moment we finally know whether you have the possibility of cross-examining that witness -- that accused or not, in relation to the -- to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's a little bit different question than I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the purpose of why we have put to you whether you make any distinction between one and the other is precisely because it could -- could have a bearing. We haven't decided anything of course as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: My suggestion would be, Judge, and it's my position that it can -- it can be, as you say, held in limbo. I don't know if that's the correct phrase, but it certainly could be. There are, for example, some passages that would just be redacted until such point in time that Mr. Borovcanin, for example, decides to take the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's another -- another issue for the discussion for today. We'll come to that later. We'll come to at that later. I think we have -- we have got the gist of your -- of your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STOLE
utterances.text: I just wonder if any of the parties are in a position to enlighten the Trial Chamber on the possible relevance of jurisprudence from the European Court of Human Rights on Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights on the principle of fair trial. I know that there is jurisprudence on the question or -- under which criteria a statement by a witness can be used in the case that he is not available for cross-examination during the trial, and if there has been no possibilities for the Defence before at pre-trial stage to -- to ask to have -- to use the right to put questions to -- to the witness, the right of contradiction, if there would be any submissions on that jurisprudence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the case I cited is -- speaks directly to Article 6, sections 1 and 3, and is a case from the European Court of Human Rights. So it does speak directly to that and discusses those -- those issues. It's the one case we could find on that -- on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Stole. I would just cite for the Court, there's another case. It's Luca, L-u-c-a, versus Italy. It's 2003 case at 36 EHRR 46. Another case is Unterpertinger versus Austria, 1986 case. Both of these cases are from the European Convention of Human Rights and the European Court of Human Rights, and they do cite Article 6. .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think this last one I'm familiar with. I don't think it deals precisely with the point we are discussing. It deals with something else that -- yes. Yes, Mr. Josse. One moment, because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I can come to Judge Stole's question in a few moments' time, if I may. Perhaps I could begin by saying that there may be some confusion, certainly there is on my part, between the use of the expression "probative value" and "admissibility." And Mr. McCloskey very carefully, and in my submission correctly drew a distinction between whether something is probative and whether something is admissible. And as I say, Your Honour, I had assumed that to be position, but Mr. McCloskey, as I've already said, answered the question very carefully. He went on in relation to, as he put it, the bigger question, the admissibility question, and said that it's an issue that he would like to brief in due course. I had rather assumed the Trial Chamber wanted to hear oral submissions upon this today, in part because in order to deal with question number two, which clearly has practical implications as to how things are going to proceed next week, you need to decide on that before we get to next week. And so I will proceed on that basis, if I may, and make these submissions: Your Honour, I'm sure the Court is well aware of the general common law rule. The general common law rule was developed for good reason, because it was thought unfair to a co-accused, and it was thought unfair because it's worth remembering that at the interview of the accused, the co-accused was not present nor represented when the accused made the interview or made the statement, interview and statement being interchangeable for this purpose. And so the account being given by the accused was not capable of challenge. And, Your Honour, my note goes on to deal with the very point that Your Honour raised; namely, the position is, of course, completely different if the accused in question, the one who gave the interview, chooses to give evidence. Because if the accused chooses to give evidence, then what the accused says is evidence in the case as a whole and is evidence in the case of all the accused. And the co-accused, through counsel, can, of course, cross-examine and challenge what the accused has said. However, in my submission, that does not, even in those circumstances, render the interview admissible, unless and until the accused adopts it in the witness box. If the accused adopts it and says, "Yes, what I said in that interview is the truth," then it becomes evidence against the co-accused, because at that point in time the co-accused are able to cross-examine and challenge it. If, on the other hand, the accused says, "What I said in the interview is not true," not necessarily in whole but in part, then it still doesn't become evidence for the very same reason, that at the time that the accused made the statement or gave the interview, perhaps I should say, the co-accused wasn't present and weren't in a position to challenge it. So that's how I contend the law should be in relation to that. Your Honour, the fundamental objection, we contend, is that any thought of admitting this statement against the co-accused would fall foul of the very Statute. We say that Article 21(4)(e) would be breached, which says: "In the determine of any charge against the accused, pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled the following minimum guarantees in full equality, and is to examine or have examine the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the conditions as witnesses against him." In reality, in our submission, this would contravene that very Article. So far as these Rules are concerned, Your Honour has rightly taken me to Rule 89(D), and I don't intend at this point to say anything more about it. Your Honour, addressing the argument that this is a piece of evidence that the Trial Chamber can assess and weigh at the end of the proceedings, we contend that that is a submission that needs to be treated with great caution. We, of course, acknowledge that the threshold for admission of evidence in this Tribunal is a relatively low one, and in particular that hearsay evidence is admissible. But this Trial Chamber in particular has been very keen, I contend, to keep an eye on that particular issue and has kept under very close control the extent and degree to which evidence can be put in, without it showing, A, it has some probative value and, B, as I say more fundamentally, it fits within the rights of the accused, as I've already described. And in my submission, it's, if I could use a colloquialism, asking for trouble to admit this, simply because -- and say at the end of the case, it will all come out in the wash and we'll work out exactly what use to make of it and how it might help, because really what the Trial Chamber need is to be quite clear as to what the Prosecution are saying its particular use is going to be. But I'm not going to stray on to that in any more detail because the Trial Chamber has said that it doesn't want to deal with it in its particular form today, and I'm quite content with that notwithstanding the e-mail that I sent yesterday. So, Your Honour, that leads me to deal briefly with the situation in various national jurisdictions. The common law position is well known, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, just before you go further, and I'm sure you can anticipate my question at this stage. Underlying the common law principle in addition to -- as a component, a big component, of the unfairness concept is the fact that hearsay, out of court statements, are not admissible, and that makes the common law rule very consistent in terms of the effect of a statement of one accused on other co-accused. But what is your submission in a Tribunal where hearsay statements are admissible, albeit the nature of them goes to their weight? What distinguishes this particular out of court statement from other forms of out of court statements that are admissible in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, unless one is going to say, as Judge Kwon has observed, that this statement is admissible through Mr. Graham, in other words, that Mr. Graham is really the witness and is simply repeating what Borovcanin has said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And let's operate on that perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because otherwise, of course, it falls foul of Rule 92. It clearly doesn't fall into any of the criteria of Rule 92. But if one is going to deal with it on that -- on that very basis, in other words, it's a hearsay statement and why is this particular piece of hearsay more admissible than any other, then I am bound to say I don't have a particular answer to that -- to that very conundrum. I accept that. Save for the fact that it's really an absurd situation, I contend, because the very maker of the statement is available. He's sitting in the courtroom, in fact. He's not compelled to give evidence under Article 21(4)(g), and it's taking the hearsay principle to an absurd and, above all else, unfair extreme. That's really what I can tell you about it. I mean, hearsay evidence needs some degree of sensible and proper and fair - I emphasise the word "fair" - regulation; and in particular, this would not be a fair regulation for the reasons as I've just described, and in particular for the submission I've made as to why Mr. -- what Mr. Borovcanin says is not capable of challenge by any of the co-accused in this case. That's the answer I give, but technically it could be said to be a piece of hearsay evidence. However, if I could say this - and it's not meant to be a threat or a war - but doesn't it invite the Defence, when this comes to our phase of the case, to put in newspaper articles, for example, by the bucketful suggesting in some way the things the Prosecution allege didn't happen, putting in all sorts of hearsay statements? For example, what about calling people, investigators who have said, "I've spoken to "X" in the field." And "X" says, "It's absolutely nonsense. This defendant wasn't at that place at that given time." It's an invitation, in my submission, to allow the Defence to basically play exactly the same game, dare I use that particular word. In my submission, hearsay evidence needs the most careful and close regulation by the Trial Chamber; otherwise, it becomes, one, a free for all and, two, a very unfair trial. Dealing briefly, if I may, with what Judge Stole said. I, too, had a note in relation to the case that Mr. Meek referred of Luca and Italy, and what was said in that case -- I'm not aware of Mr. McCloskey's case. I'm not saying it don't exist, but I haven't read it. But what was said in Luca that is relevant, and I can read it: "If the defendant has been given an adequate and proper opportunity to challenge the depositions, either when made or at a later stage, their admission in evidence will not in itself contravene Article 6(1) and Article 6(3)(d). That's obviously of the convention. The corollary of that, however, is that where the conviction is based solely or to a decisive degree on depositions that have been made by a person whom the accused has had no opportunity to examine or have examined, whether during the investigation or at trial. The rights of the Defence are restricted to an extent that is incompatible which the guarantees provided by Article 6. I'm not going to spend very much more time on domestic jurisdictions. I could, of course, talk about the law in England. I based, understandably, many of the submissions I've already made on the law in England. In the United States, and no doubt Mr. Meek will correct me if I'm wrong about this, the matter is governed by the Sixth Amendment of the United States Constitution, where it says: "In all criminal proceedings, the accused should enjoy the right to be confronted with the witnesses against him," I'm paraphrasing it slightly, "and the Supreme Court has held that in substitution for oral evidence, the maker of a statement can only be admitted if two conditions are satisfied: First, the accused must have been afforded the right to confront the witness at some stage, if not at trial; and second, it must be shown the witness is unavailable to give evidence at trial." And I've already dealt with the second point. I also understand, Your Honours, and I'm certainly not an authority on this, to put it mildly, but broadly speaking, the same law applies in the Netherlands by -- by virtue apparently of Article 341, subsection 3 of the Netherlands Code of Criminal Procedure. A statement made by an accused is admissible only against the accused who made the statement. And that's been apparently affirmed by the Netherlands Supreme Court. Before I sit down, I would like to deal with one other matter, which both Mr. McCloskey referred to, and Ms. Fauveau as well, and that is Mr. McCloskey's concession in relation to this matter in the Blagojevic and Jokic case. And I would like if I may, in fact, to hand out that concession, because it's all well and good for him to say, "Well, the law's moved on and I made that concession based on the law as it then stood," but it was unambiguous and a robust concession at that time. And I'm going to hand out the filing. Normally, I would simply have cited it in the course of an argument. If I could have a moment. Yes. I'm told by Mr. Krgovic that it's time for the break. I'll be about another five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have only got five minutes left, I think we can finish with your submissions; then we can have the break, of course, with the indulgence of everyone here, and then we would like to know who else would like to address the Trial Chamber on these issues. So please proceed for about five minutes, and then we'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful to Mr. Meek. It shows how dangerous it is for an English lawyer to talk about American law. Apparently, it was the Sixth Amendment to the Bill of Rights, not the Constitution. I imagine to an American, quite an important difference. But, Your Honour, I've handed up the filing of Mr. McCloskey, dated the 30th of June, 2003, in the Blagojevic and Jokic case. I'm not going to read through it all now, by any means. The relevant paragraphs are paragraphs 13 to 21, and I would invite the Trial Chamber to read those paragraphs carefully in due course, because Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a copy of this scandalous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm not going to read through it now, Your Honour. Your Honour, the legal officer would like one. I do have another copy. And to some extent, in the course of this filing, Mr. McCloskey doesn't just make the concession, but he explains why he's making the concession, and I would adopt and endorse the very learned words of Mr. McCloskey in this particular filing. I think, as I say, I can save some time by not reading through any of the relevant passages, but I would ask the Chamber to pay close attention to it, and I ask Mr. McCloskey rhetorically, through Your Honours, what exactly has changed since he made the clear and very fair concession that he did in that particular case. So, Your Honour, those really are the submissions that I make in relation to this particular issue. If I can help further, I'd be only too glad to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we break, who else wishes to address the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to just for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I would also like to address the Chamber for about ten minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very briefly because basically this topic is more related to other co-accused than to us, but we would like to heard, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I may, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we stand a chance of not even finishing the first the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Half an hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's continue with this very interesting discussion, which will not finish today because there are also other points that we have indicated to you we would like to hear submissions upon. That will be tomorrow, of course, again, 9.00 in the morning. After Mr. Josse, who would like to go next? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try not to be repetitive, and I'll try to be very brief. So I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are a wise man, because you have anticipated the consequences, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just received my submission on the admissibility of the parts of statements of an accused related to the other accused. This is multi-accused trial, and it implies that the rights of all accused must be respected. It includes the right of the accused not to testify in his own trial, in his own case, and the right of the other accused to cross-examine the witnesses against him. It is our position that the statement is admissible just if the rights of all co-accused are respected, unless the nature of cause arises. In this case, in the case that the lack of cross-examination results from the right of the other co-accused, the right not to testify in his case, such statement could not be admissible because it would violate the rights of co-accused. It is our position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, for repeating but not much. Who is next? I understood that Mr. Lazarevic wanted to address us. Mr. Haynes wanted to address us. Ms. Nikolic. Who wishes to go next? Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is very brief one. There is one thing that I believe Trial Chamber should have -- should take into consideration when assessing all the arguments that have been raised regarding this issue, and that's the nature of the indictment against not just Mr. Borovcanin but against all the accused. This is a case with multiple accused but also case in which they are all charged with participation in a joint criminal enterprise, and I believe that these -- these facts should be taken into account when assessing all these arguments. Each and every of the accused is charged for acts and conducts of all the other participants in the joint criminal enterprise. So I believe that it would be really unfair, even if Mr. Borovcanin mentions himself in his interviews, which he does, I have nothing to hide, that even such mentioning would have certain impact on other co-accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Ms. Nikolic. Or Mr. Bourgon. I don't know who had the intention of addressing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President. We support and join in the submissions that have been expressed so far with respect to the conclusion that anything -- any probative value which can be attached to parts of the statement made by one accused in this case should not be considered against the other accused. We limit our submissions to the fact that the important issue is acts and conduct of any of the co-accused; and secondly, that this is a fair trial issue based on the right to confront the source. And the last thing is what is important to us is the reliability of the source. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very, very briefly, Mr. President. The position in the law of North America, if -- if the Canadians and US citizens don't mind being lumped together for those purposes appears to me to be properly summarised as this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I need consultation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Incriminating inculpatory extra-judicial declarations of a co-accused made in the absence or without the knowledge of the accused are inadmissible in evidence in a criminal trial to prove the guilt of one other than the declarant. That, I can confirm is the position in the common law jurisdictions with which I'm familiar. The European Court of Human Rights in the case of Luca and Italy said as follows and it seems to be precisely the point that Judge Stole has in mind: If the defendant has been given an adequate and proper to challenge the depositions either when made or at a later stage, their admission in evidence will not in itself contravene Article 6. The corollary of that, however, is that where a conviction is based solely or to a decisive degree on depositions that have been made by a person whom the accused has had no opportunity to examine or to have examined whether during the investigation or at the trial, the rights of the Defence are restricted to an extent that is incompatible with the guarantees provided by Article 6. And I submit that the practice of this Tribunal to date as evidenced by the concession of Mr. McCloskey in a previous trial concerning the same facts all point in the same direction, that the rule at common law, the rule in American law and the jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights has spoken with one voice for many, many years now. Of course this is a Tribunal that admits hearsay evidence but my submission in answer to Judge Prost's question is really this: Interviews under caution of suspects are a separate and very special category of hearsay evidence which are governed by special rules and procedures in virtually every jurisdiction all over the globe, including this one. To adopt something Mr. Josse said, it is really stretching logic to the extreme to say that a man who is sitting in a room with an investigator and a chief Prosecutor, knowing that he is under suspicion for genocide and crimes against humanity is in the real sense of the word willing to be there and giving a similar account to somebody who might be making a witness statement which is read out to a court. There is very good reason why we guard against allowing into evidence what people in those situations say about the acts, conducts, and criminal conduct of others. It is easy and convenient for them so to do, and that's why we've guarded against it down the years, and I submit there is no good reason for doing so -- from departing from that rule now. Of course the situation might be different as to the probative value of those statements in the interview if the declarant, in this case Mr. Borovcanin, gives evidence. But let's cross that bridge when we get to it. And I've been involved in trials of this sort for well over 20 years now, and the way in which we deal with that is we present a redacted or edited version of the interview at this stage, and if Mr. Borovcanin goes into the witness box, Mr. McCloskey could, without any sensible objection, produce the full version of the interview and cross-examine him on everything he had to say about the other accused in the dock. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. -- before -- before I give you the floor, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Haynes, reference to the Luca versus Italy case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What inferences if at all do you draw from the use by the European Court of Human Rights of the words where a conviction is based solely or to a decisive degree on depositions of a person, et cetera, solely or a desire -- what difference do you draw in relation to those instances where the conviction is not based solely or to a decisive degree on -- on such a statement but such a statement is one other fruit in the basket?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A valid point. The difference of course is with Luca versus Italy, it is a decision of the European Court of Human Rights based on the conviction of a man, so necessarily they're looking back on events. What I draw from that case is the principle that Article 6 -- excuse me a minute. I've lost it on my screen here. Article 6 really forbids provisions which lead to the conviction of people where they do not have the rights to a fair trial enshrined therein and set out in the decision. If that decision, I submit, had been made before Mr. Luka had stood his trial, his trial would not have take the same course, and the evidence against him would not have been adduced. That's what I submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you Mr. Haynes. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could speak briefly to these cases and the Strasbourg court decisions. I'm learning more as we go because we've -- as you know, we're -- this was relatively new but I do think the Strasbourg court and the Convention is extremely important authority for you to look at. The Article that they're speaking of, Article 6 at section 3, and it says, everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights, and then section D, to examine or have examined witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him. So the right to cross-examine witnesses. In addition, in a September 4, 2007, case of Gosa versus Poland, the court points out something that they have apparently reiterated quite a bit. 942007.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can't imagine the European Court uses US dating, but thank you for bringing me to the present. That's -- all right. The point I wanted to make was that on page 15 of the decision it says, "The Court reiterates that the admissibility of evidence is primarily a matter for regulation by national law and as a general rule it is for the national courts to assess the evidence before them. The Court's task under the Convention is not to give a ruling as to whether statements or witnesses were properly admitted as evidence but, rather, to ascertain whether the proceedings as a whole, including the way in which evidence was taken, were fair." And that goes directly to what I had said earlier that it is your -- that's what you're determining under 89(D), I believe. Now, the case that I spoke to earlier from 2007, Carta, is in French, but I have a rough outline of the holding that goes directly to your question, Mr. President, and that is a case where -- it was an Italian case where a statement of a co-accused was allowed to be used against another accused, and that found its way to Strasbourg and the Strasbourg court found that that was not a violation of Article 6, and -- and in their holding states that it had not been the sole piece of evidence to convict the person, that it had been corroborated by other evidence, and that the other accused had had the right to challenge the information that came out of that interview. This same holding was part of the Gosa versus Poland case that I mentioned, and last -- but I should state before that the Italian case, Italy changed its law and said this -- that you could not use statements against co-accused. So Italy fixed their -- in their view, their domestic situation, but the Strasbourg court said it did not violate Article 6. So just to make that -- that clear. And the -- we found a case out of Norway. We didn't find any cases from Malta, unfortunately, but we did find a case from Norway that is called case of Kaste and Mathisen versus Norway against -- 2007, and in that case they found that the statement of the co-accused went to -- was the sole bit of evidence, so they found it did violate Article 6. So -- and we will give you those cases, and I think in the future you'll find that this is a very important source of authority, because it tracks so closely with who we are and what we're trying to do. Though I also wanted to point out that some of the factors we're looking at, you really won't be able to evaluate until you see the whole interview. So -- and I imagine that you're not going to be making this decision regarding whether or not the interview can be used against other accused until you've had a chance to see the whole interview, though that hadn't -- we haven't discussed that. But in order to determine the information in that interview, I can tell you it's not -- it's not the sole evidence about anything. In fact, just generally I don't believe Mr. Borovcanin blames anyone is my recollection of it, but he does mention others. So I believe that this will be decided on a later date when everyone has had a chance to more fully brief it. But I do have question two in front of me, and we can get directly to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we close the discussion on point one, question one? Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just want to make something clarify -- clarify something. That Italian case I don't think refers to a statement of a co-accused but a witness who became inaccessible during the hearing. In my opinion, therefore, it is a completely different situation and a completely different matter, because my argument was that a statement or an interview of the co-accused is completely different from any other statement by any other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll into these cases when -- when the time arrives. As regards my country, you're not going to find anything because the rule is absolute, and of course the Prosecution would try to obviate by separating co-accused and trying them separately, and in that case the other issue will arise whether the statement of an accomplice can be the basis, the sole basis for a conviction unless it is -- in case it's not corroborated, and our law specifically states that it needs corroboration except in certain -- in relation to certain crimes, drug-related crimes. Okay. So I think we can safely go to the second part. And the second question, which shouldn't engage us too much, is the following: If we were to determine that the evidence should have probative value with respect to the other accused, what would be the permissible scope of the submissions on and cross-examination of Witness number 3 by the other accused at the stage of the proceedings where admissibility is to be determined? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd just like to intervene at this time. There are two quick issues we need to bring forward today that are unrelated to this second debate, and this will require five minutes. Just to let you know, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The first issue, Mr. President, is -- refers to the Defence submissions concerning the admissibility of proposed intercept evidence. After filing our submissions late on Monday night, I found out that I filed the wrong annex with my motion. I informed the Prosecution, and the only change is in the last column of that annex, and we'd just like to inform the Court that we will be filing the proper annex that should have been filed at that time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it there would not be any objection on your part, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just very briefly I would like to address the Chamber related to the submission, the written submission we filed regarding Witness 108 and the accompanying material and the possible hearing of this witness next week. Our Defence is investing great efforts to complete our investigation and prepare properly for the cross-examination of this witness. We have heard a great number of witnesses and acquired a documentation but we still have a lot of work to do in order to be adequately prepared for this cross-examination. I will be completely frank with the Chamber, as I have been with my learned friends in the Prosecution, and I would appreciate it if we could move into private session for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the submission filed by the Defence team of Mr. Nikolic regarding the 68 material before the questioning of this witness I hope we will receive today by the end of the day what else has been discovered in this case. Our Defence withdraws the submission and we will continue to discuss with our colleagues from the Prosecution. The time we need to complete our investigation, which is time and effort-consuming is such that it would be actually adequate to bring this witness after the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Nikolic. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further. I think I have said what I needed to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in private session. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have had a chance to speak with counsel, and we understand their concerns, and we have agreed not to object and to leave this matter in the -- in your hands. We know that it's -- it's a difficult situation to -- having witnesses not -- not here, but as I say, we have good communication and a good relationship, and I think in the end that has benefited this trial, and it's the speed and the efficiency by which we've been able to work together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And where would that leave us, Madam Registrar? If we could have the list of witnesses for this coming week. Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll give you a decision later. We have still got six minutes. Perhaps you can start on the second posit that we made, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think I can deal with that in the time. And as I think I alluded to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me ask you this. If Witness 108 who was due to testify on Tuesday, start testifying on Tuesday, will come later, would you still wait to get Mr. Graham to testify until Friday? Wednesday. I see, I see, I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We may be able to move that -- move him up. We're not sitting Monday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he still work with the -- with the OTP or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. He's with the -- I believe the Manchester police department. But he will be here over the weekend, and I will -- I think we should be able to be prepared on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One thing I also forgot to mention regarding 108, it's Mr. Nicholls is handling that witness. We need to contact that witness and see, because we brought him here once. We need to make sure that he's okay with that -- okay. All right. We've done that, and he is okay with that, so we're all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you can remain standing, Mr. McCloskey. Your position on number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think as I alluded to, was it yesterday or a previous day, that with the particular law and our particular institution, I -- I don't think the traditional notions of standing need to be applied as strictly as they may, so I would not be objecting to cross-examination by any party that felt they had an interest in cross-examining Alistair Graham, but I would request that -- that it be a legal interest and that legal interest be identified in advance of the cross-examination so that it is something that we're prepared to deal with as is normal for, you know, items associated with law, and it not become a general attack on Mr. Graham. He was the lead investigator after Mr. Ruez for a few years, and as you can imagine, there may be Defence counsel that want to go into other areas. But if we can limit it to the legal issue at hand, and as other people feel affected by what may have come out of that interview, I don't have an objection to that, and that would be my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Who wishes -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you had mentioned the other day a distinction between matters that are personal to Mr. Borovcanin versus matters more general such as compliance with the rules. I'm taking it now you're not necessarily insisting on that strict division and that you would not be taking a position with respect to general questioning by the Defence on all such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would -- I would insist on relevance, I think, and to the degree that I -- and I've spoken to counsel after that and heard their view on -- on, for example, whether or not there was coercion involved. And if it was an issue that was very particular to -- to Mr. Borovcanin and counsel and a position they were taking, I think it may not be relevant for others to -- to get into that, in which case I may object, but I think your discretion to determine what is relevant and what is not is -- is fine, and I wouldn't go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Which Defence team wishes to address this posit? Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be lying if I said I was too concerned about this, but having said that, to use one of my favourite expressions, what's good for the goose is good for the gander. If the Trial Chamber decide that this interview is or may be admissible against the co-accused, then in my submission we are entitled to challenge it in any way we so choose. The Prosecution really cannot have their cake and eat it. They can't on the one hand say it's evidence, it's evidence against you, your client, but you can't then challenge it root and branch, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: That's three expressions in two sentences, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Apologies to the interpreters, because I suspect I'm not making their life very easy at the moment. Your Honour, if I could take an extreme example, we would submit that we would be entitled to ask for a voir dire on the admissibility of this particular interview and that Mr. Borovcanin would be a compellable witness for the co-accused in the course of that voir dire, that voir dire being a trial within a trial and not being part of the main trial, and indeed if the Trial Chamber rule against us on one, then that's something we'd contemplate on two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd anticipated this as a voir dire also, and I don't -- and I am I'm not saying that -- or trying to suggest that they can't challenge it as they can. Regarding Mr. Borovcanin, I will leave that to another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And we have to leave our discussion to another day as well. We are going to adjourn now until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Do you wish to address the Chamber, Madam Fauveau? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, very briefly, and to -- I don't want to leave the impression that I wanted to mislead you. When I spoke about that case that at the moment the witness gave the statement, he was a witness. It was later he became a co-accused. I don't want you to believe that I tried to mislead you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I said, we will go through those judgements, at least two of which I am familiar with in any case. So we stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
